course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: The Constitution
lesson.summary: How the Constitution created a limited but dynamic national government through federalism and the separation of powers, and what it kept and changed from the Articles and from colonial government.
learningGoals: Explain how federalism divides power between the national and state governments.
Explain how the separation of powers and checks and balances limit the national government.
Explain the continuities and changes between the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution.
lesson.bigIdea: The Constitution created a limited but dynamic central government that embodied federalism and provided for a separation of powers among three branches.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain continuities and changes in the structure and functions of government with ratification of the Constitution. For each feature, ask what it kept from earlier governments and what it changed.

sections.title: Federalism

blocks.text: Delegates from the states participated in the Constitutional Convention that created a limited but dynamic central government embodying federalism. Federalism divides power between the national government and the states. The Constitution gave Congress specific powers, which are called enumerated powers. Article I, Section 8 included the power to lay and collect taxes, to borrow money, and to regulate commerce with foreign nations, among the states, and with the Indian tribes. It also gave Congress the power to make all laws “necessary and proper” to carry out those powers, a clause that allowed the national government to grow in later years.

The Constitution declared itself the supreme law of the land, which meant that valid federal law overrode conflicting state law. Powers not given to the national government remained with the states or the people, a principle later stated in the Tenth Amendment. States kept responsibility for much of daily life, including most criminal law, education, and local government.

sections.takeaway: Federalism shares power between the national and state governments and gives the national government specific powers, including taxation and the regulation of commerce.

sections.title: Separation of powers and checks and balances
sections.conceptTitle: Separation of powers and checks and balances

blocks.text: The Constitution provided for a separation of powers among three branches. Congress, which makes laws, is divided into a House of Representatives and a Senate. The president, who carries out the laws, is chosen by an Electoral College, and the federal courts interpret the law. Each branch can check the others. The president can veto bills, Congress can override a veto and can impeach officials, the Senate approves treaties and appointments, including federal judges, and the courts decide cases under the Constitution and federal law.

These arrangements reflected the fear of concentrated power that Revolutionary leaders had learned from republican thinkers and from Montesquieu. They also limited excessive popular influence. Senators were chosen by state legislatures and presidents were chosen by electors rather than by direct vote, so only the House was elected directly by voters.
The process of amending the Constitution was made difficult but not impossible, which allowed it to change over time.

sections.takeaway: Three branches with checks on one another limit the power of each, and indirect election limited the influence of popular majorities.

sections.title: Continuities and changes from the Articles
sections.conceptTitle: Continuities and changes from the Articles

blocks.text: The Constitution kept the republican form of government, the written framework, the states, and a Congress, and it kept many familiar features of colonial and state government, such as elected legislatures with two houses and a division of powers. The Constitution changed the structure of the national government. It created an executive and a national court system, gave the national government direct power to tax and to regulate commerce among the states, provided that federal law was supreme over state law, and replaced one vote per state with representation in the House based on population.

Ratification therefore preserved the republican ideals of the Revolution while correcting the weaknesses that the Articles had shown. Its supporters considered it a stronger government that nonetheless remained limited by law.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: The Constitution did not abolish state governments. It created a stronger national government on top of state governments that kept real power.

sections.takeaway: The Constitution kept the republic and the states but gave the national government the structure and powers that the Articles had lacked.

connections.title: Putting the Constitution into practice
connections.body: The Constitution's words had to be turned into working government. Topic 3.10 follows the presidencies of Washington and Adams and the first political parties.
connections.transferQuestion: Which feature of the Constitution do you think was the biggest change from the Articles of Confederation, and why?
connections.feedback: A strong answer names a specific feature, such as the power to tax or the creation of an executive, and ties it to a problem under the Articles.
